subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 11 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy — and well done, because this is the last unit of Year 2! There is no new software to learn; instead you talk, sort, and play a game to explore three big ideas: what computers are good at, how people pick the right device, and the difference between real robots and the make-believe robots we see in films. The first idea is that computers can do some things better than people. A computer is very fast, it never gets tired or bored, it can store a whole library of books inside one small machine, and it follows instructions exactly. The second idea is that people choose different computer devices for different reasons. A desktop is powerful with a large screen, but heavy; a laptop, a tablet and a smartphone are smaller and easy to carry. The best device depends on what you need it for and where you are.

outcomes: Name some tasks computers can do better than people — work fast, never get tired or bored, store a lot, and follow instructions exactly.
Understand that people are still better at some things, like making up something new (a story, a picture, a joke).
Know that people use different computer devices — desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone.
Give a simple reason for choosing a device (for example, "a tablet is light and easy to carry").
Say what a robot is — a machine that does a task without help from a person.
Tell the difference between a real robot and a fictional (make-believe) robot.
Give the robot a short, correct sequence of steps to reach a place, and understand a robot does exactly what it is told.
Find and fix a wrong step in a short set of robot instructions.

concepts.title: What computers can do better than us
concepts.explanation:
Computers can do some things better than people. A computer is very fast, it never gets tired or bored, it can store a huge amount in a small space, and it follows instructions exactly. But people are still better at some things, like making up something brand new.

Who is quicker? Layla adds two numbers in her head. A computer adds the same two numbers. Who finishes first? Now there are ten numbers. now a hundred!
concepts.example: Who finishes first now? Then share the four ideas, one at a time, in one friendly sentence each: “A computer is very fast.” “A computer never gets tired or bored — it can work all day and night.” “A computer can store a whole library of books inside one small machine.” “A computer follows instructions exactly — it does just what it is told.”
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name one thing a person does better (make up something new)? Can you name one or two things a computer does better than a person (fast, never tired, stores a lot)?

concepts.title: Choosing the right device
concepts.explanation: People use different computer devices, and you choose one for a reason. A desktop is powerful with a big screen, but it is heavy and stays on the desk. A laptop, a tablet and a smartphone are smaller and easy to carry. The best choice depends on what you need it for and where you are. A desktop is big and strong — good for someone who sits at a desk all day. A laptop folds up and comes with you — good for travelling.
concepts.example: A tablet is light with a nice big screen — good for a delivery driver. A smartphone fits in your pocket and joins the internet almost anywhere.
concepts.checkYourself: a tablet is easy to carry. a desktop has a big screen. The reason matters more than the exact device.

concepts.title: Real robots and make-believe robots
concepts.explanation: A robot is a machine that does a task without help from a person. Robots in films are fictional — make-believe. Fictional robots look, speak and act like people. Real robots often do not look like people; many are just an arm or a box. Real robots repeat the same task, work in factories, go into space, and do dangerous jobs to keep people safe. Do you remember what a robot is? Then split the world into two. Some robots are only in stories and films — they are fictional, or make-believe. They talk and walk like people, but they are not real. Real robots are all around the world doing real jobs. A robot arm builds cars in a factory. A robot vacuum cleans a floor. A space robot explores places too dangerous for people.
concepts.example: Real robots often look like a machine, not a person. Real, or make-believe?
concepts.checkYourself: a real one does not talk. a make-believe one looks like a person. Can you know a robot is a machine and cannot feel?

concepts.title: The Robot Game: a robot follows exact steps
concepts.explanation: A robot does exactly what it is told — no more, no less. It cannot think for itself. So our instructions must be clear and in the right order. If one step is wrong, the robot goes the wrong way — and it is our job to find the wrong step and fix it. Lay a small grid on the floor and put a park picture on the finish square. One child stands on the START square as the robot.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.
